title: Barnard College Student Slashed in Random Attack Outside of NYC Dorm Building
content:
A student at Barnard College was slashed outside of her New York City dorm building during a seemingly random attack.

Police said that the attacker snuck up behind the victim while she was walking in front of the suite-style Barnard residence hall on West 116th Street around 8:15 p.m. on Thursday, November 12, the New York City Police Department confirmed to Us. The victim – who has not been publicly identified but was said to be a 21-year-old woman – was cut behind the ear.

The victim was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center for treatment, and she is currently in stable condition.

Following the attack, Barnard College notified students by sending them an email confirming that the victim is a “member of the Barnard community,” according to The Columbia Spectator.

Olivia Rodrigo Slams Cornell After Alleged Gang Rape: 'Stand With Jane Doe'

Columbia University and Barnard College are directly adjacent to each other and are located in Manhattan’s Morningside Heights neighborhood.

The incident was witnessed by pedestrians, and student Eva Kates told Columbia University’s newspaper that she was walking home when she saw the victim and police after they responded to the scene in the aftermath of the slashing.

“I originally thought that someone had robbed Morton Williams and I was like, ‘Wow, they have a lot of police officers for that,’” Kates recalled. “But then I saw a girl, and she had blood on her neck.”

She added, “I was walking down 116th, and there were a bunch of police officers, at least five or six, standing there.”

Columbia University students received texts about the suspect, who was described as a “dark skin male, 5-foot-9, stocky build wearing a black hooded coat with a yellow hat underneath and tan pants,” according to the university’s newspaper.

The suspect fled the scene and no suspects have been arrested as of time of publication.

Brown University Shares Plans to Reevaluates Safety Policies After Shooting

Gary Maroni, director of Barnard’s Community Accountability, Response, and Emergency Services department, also sent a text update to students, first notifying them that the attack took place on Thursday at 9:30 p.m.

Maroni later sent a follow-up email to Barnard students at 10:19 p.m., in which he shared an image of the suspect that was captured by a security camera. He also confirmed to students and community members that the New York Police Department was investigating the incident.

The investigation into the attack remains ongoing as authorities work to track down the slasher and bring him into custody. The New York Police Department had no additional information to share when contacted by Us about the case.

title: Beyonce Shares Rare Details About Her and Jay-Z's Intimate Wedding
content:
Beyoncé is sharing rare insight into her wedding with Jay-Z 18 years after they tied the knot.

“We had a very small wedding in our home,” the “Texas Hold ‘Em” singer, 45, told i-D in an interview published on Wednesday, November 11. “We told the guests we were having a party, and no one knew they were coming to our wedding but our parents and a few friends.”

Beyoncé also gushed about her wedding dress, which her mother, Tina Knowles, designed.

“My favorite dress my mother designed was my wedding dress — it was gorgeously simple and made with her love,” she said. “Wearing a dress she designed was very important to me, and more important than any designer dress.”

Beyonce and Jay-Z’s Rare Family Photos With Blue Ivy, Rumi and Sir

Beyoncé and Jay-Z, 56, tied the knot at their New York City home in April 2008. Though the couple have mostly kept quiet about their special day, a few details have been made public over the years.

People reported earlier this year that the Grammy winners traveled to upstate New York days before their nuptials to quietly obtain their marriage license. The pair chose April 4 as their wedding date because of the personal significance of the number four. (Beyoncé was born on September 4, while Jay-Z was born on December 4.)

Only 40 guests attended the ceremony, including Kelly Rowland, Michelle Williams, Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin. Beyoncé’s parents and sister, Solange, were also on the guest list, as well as Jay-Z’s mom, grandmother, sister and niece.

Look Back at Beyonce's Met Gala Style Evolution Amid Her Return After 10 Years

Beyoncé’s mother’s minister, Rudy Rasmus, officiated the wedding, while DJ Cassidy provided the music at the reception.

Beyoncé finally gave fans a look at her wedding dress in the 2011 video for her song “I Was Here.” The stunning gown featured a strapless design and a dramatic, ruffled train.

Nearly four years after tying the knot, Beyoncé and Jay-Z welcomed their first child, daughter Blue Ivy, in January 2012. The pair became parents again when they welcomed twins Rumi and Sir in June 2017.

In her i-D interview, which promoted the British launch of her haircare brand Cécred, Beyoncé gushed about her children developing their own sense of fashion.

“I’m so excited to pass all my archives to my kids, especially now that they’re all discovering their own personal style,” she shared. “I’m going to enjoy seeing how they pull from their parents’ carpets and tours if they’re ever interested. Rumi’s favourite place to shop right now is Ross and TJ Maxx these days.”

title: Candace Cameron Bure Addresses Marriage Dynamic After 'Special Forces' Comment
content:
Candace Cameron Bure and Valeri Bure have cracked the code to a long-lasting marriage, recently celebrating their milestone 30th anniversary.

“Without our faith, I don’t think we would have the marriage the way it is today. That’s kind of our secret, and the way that we approach everything,” Valeri, 52, exclusively told Us during a joint interview with Candace, 50, in celebration of passing selection on Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test season 5. “Our family is very important to us, and our faith is important. That’s what brings us all together.”

And with their shared foundation of faith, Valeri also joked that there’s another secret to their happy and loving union.

“Is it PG or not? I have a couple secrets, and our kids do not want to hear those secrets,” he quipped to Us, while Candace chimed in to add, “He’s funny. Makes me laugh.”

Candace Cameron Bure's Best Quotes About Her Marriage to Valeri Bure

Candace gushed that her husband’s humor is “the best thing,” adding that she and Valeri crack up about “all the dumb little things” constantly.

“That’s just the best part because I think you have to laugh in life,” she said. “So to have your best friend that continues to make you laugh is great.”

Valeri, meanwhile, shared that he appreciates learning something new about Candace daily and how she “continues to change.”

“That’s the fun part about it, is that our journeys continue to go forward and not be like, ‘Oh my gosh, OK, you’re the same person that you were 30 years ago,’” he said.

Candace Cameron Bure and Husband Valeri Bure's Relationship Timeline

In their more than three decades together, Candace and Valeri have raised three children — daughter Natasha, 28, and sons Lev, 26, and Maksim, 24 — and are now navigating the new world of grandparenthood. (Lev and wife Elliott Bure welcomed son Bond Leo in September while Natasha and husband Bradley Steven Perry announced the arrival of daughter Winnie in October.)

“Candace is a baby hogger. She is the worst. I would hold my grandkid and she would run up and just start taking it away and I’m like, ‘Stop, stop!’ I’m like, ‘This is my turn to hold the baby.’ So, I’ve learned that she is a baby hogger. She’s taking it away from me,” Valeri joked to Us.

Candace agreed with her husband’s assessment. “It’s true. I do. But the kids have all said, like, ‘What happened to you? Who’s become a softie?’” she said. “They’re like, ‘This is not our papa that we grew up with. Who is this person?’”

“I’m like, ‘Why is your baby crying? Give it to me. Baby should not be crying,’” Valeri said, while Candace added, “I know. And our kids it’s like, ‘Nope, they gotta cry it out. Gotta cry it out.’ No crying for the grandbabies.”

Dating! Clapbacks! Candace Cameron Bure's Best Parenting Quotes

While embracing their new chapter as grandparents, Candace is also celebrating passing selection on Special Forces season 5 alongside Collin Gosselin and Alexia Umansky. Before being crowned one of the newest winners, Candace got emotional in interrogation about the dynamics in her marriage — sharing that she felt like a “beta” living with an “alpha.” Looking back, Candace shared that she felt like it was “an interesting comment” because the interrogation interviews “are so long.”

“And then they’re cut down to this 30 second clip or this one-minute clip, and it doesn’t quite paint the full story,” she explained to Us. “But we are great partners. I would say that we both lead in what we’re good at leading in and what we’re kind of meant to do. I feel so protected and loved by Val and that’s what I want. I don’t want to lead people on a mission and have to yell. I am not a protector in that way.”

Candace, however, thinks she does “very well” leading in more of a “nurturing” and “quiet” way.

“We need leaders that lead in different ways. Every type of leader has a place, but not every leader is the most commanding person. I don’t know, that’s what I think. I wish that was told in the interview because that’s kind of what we talked about, but you didn’t get to see it all,” she said, while Valeri added with a laugh, “They cut it … She’ll write a book about it.”

title: The King is Back: ‘Godzilla: Minus Zero’ Spoiler-Free Review – ScreenHub Entertainment
content:
Note: I’m going to be as spoiler-free as possible for this review. Nothing that’s not revealed in the trailers. If it sounds vague and full of holes, this is for you!

Godzilla: Minus One was a surprise hit, both for fans and Toho. It took the familiar Godzilla story and rebooted it for modern audiences. Unlike the Monsterverse going on at Warner, Minus One prioritized drama and character; these people just so happen to live in a world where Godzilla exists. So it’s not so surprising that a sequel has come about: Japan’s first feature film shot for IMAX, and thanks to the success of its predecessor, now has a wide release. So, does lightning strike twice for the franchise, or does Godzilla: Minus Zero suffer from sequelitis? Let’s find out.

Two years have passed since the events of Minus One, and Japan is still coming to grips with both emerging from the ashes of WWII and the carnage laid waste by Godzilla, seemingly defeated at the end of the last movie. But something happens that unleashes a catastrophic danger on the people of Japan and questions emerge about what to do next that’s best for the country and its people. Vague, I know, but it’s for the best.

A lot of the cast from the original film return. Ryunosuke Kamiki is front and center as Kōichi Shikishima, the pilot from the last film. He’s found happiness at long last, having married Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and accepted the role as father to the orphan Akiko, the orphaned child they both took in. Shikishima was plagued by survivor’s guilt in the first film, but has a new lease on life, which makes this new tragedy that much more impactful for him: he has something to lose now.

Other characters, such as Akitsu, the captain of the Shinsei Maru and Mizushima, his crewmate, have significantly reduced roles this time around. This is because the movie diverts a lot of screen time towards Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), the brilliant scientist turned director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau. Noda finds himself in a situation where the greater moral good is bogged down by what’s easy, and his arc more than a couple of times reminded me of Oppenheimer. A brilliant mind who has been put into a situation where he has become death, destroyer of worlds. Reinforcing this theme is the new character Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), a biologist and survivor of Hiroshima. Whereas Minus One delved into themes of life and death, Minus Zero taps into the moral grey zone of power, destruction, and retribution. There’s a fantastic, and horrifying, sequence revolving around Murakami that may just be the highlight of the movie that very much taps into the fears of atomic warfare.

It doesn’t always hit the same highs as Minus One did, that said. It does take a bit of time for the characterization and themes to really get going, and some plot points get resolved far too quickly. The depiction of the US characters also felt very cartoony. But Minus Zero is still poignant and even touching, with a lot of heart and questions to pose to the audience. So if you liked your Godzilla movie with a lot of characters you actually care about, Minus Zero continues that.

But what of the monster mayhem? There isn’t as much as you might think there would be, but what there is, is great. Let’s just say the movie wastes no time getting into it. The film really dives into that sense of scale, and that’s only bolstered by the IMAX presentation. Some of the VFX for trivial things, like birds or green-screen backgrounds while characters are on a motorcycle are jarringly rough, but rest assured, it delivers when it matters most. One sequence involving planes in the first half of the movie, was a particular highlight for me. Where the film doesn’t miss a beat though is both the score and the sound effects. Chef’s kiss. When that iconic Godzilla theme kicks in, you know you’re in for a treat.

Godzilla: Minus Zero is definitely bigger, not per se better, but still a great movie nonetheless. It keeps the story focused on its compelling characters and themes, while having them exist in these larger-than-life moments. Here’s hoping for one more Minus film to close out this story!

title: A Familiar Yet Compelling Crime Drama: ‘Paper Tiger’ Spoiler-Free Review – ScreenHub Entertainment
content:
Paper Tiger had its premiere earlier this year at the Cannes Film Festival, where it competed for the coveted Palme d’Or. A crime epic, it seeks to capture the feel and tension found in so many iconic crime films. But does it stick the landing? Let’s find out.

The film stars Miles Teller as Irwin Pearl, an engineer who ends up teaming up with his brother Gary (Adam Driver), a former NYPD officer, in establishing a lucrative side business on the docks. Of course,  nothing goes to plan, and the family quickly find themselves on the wrong side of the Russian mafia. With his wife, Ester (Scarlet Johansson) and their two sons in danger, Irwin and Gary have to find a way to keep the family safe and keep the mob off their backs.

Paper Tigers is a solid crime thriller that’s well acted and well directed. Its main roadblock is that it doesn’t really feel like it’s breaking too far from the mould, which can result in some predictability. I’ve seen variations of this film before, about a family who has gotten in way too over their head with the criminal underworld, whether intentionally or not.

Paper Tigers does at least shine, that said, especially in the acting department. Teller and Driver do great work as brothers who find their bond tested as the threat of harm and violence becomes their new reality. But it’s Johansson who excels as Ester, a frightened mother of two teenage boys. She’s rightfully scared to death, and the unexpected proximity to danger coming from her unassuming husband only makes the situation that much more baffling. Irwin isn’t a bad guy; he has no connections to crime, so the Russian mob showing up in their lives was likely the last thing on her mind.

The film also excels at bringing 1980s Queens, New York, to life. The film feels run-down, dirty, and lived-in, from the suburban home that the Pearl family lives in to the busy streets in town. In fact, both the aesthetic and criminal elements reminded me in part of Grand Theft Auto IV and Niko’s early interactions with the Russian mob in that universe’s equivalent of Brooklyn and Queens.

In the end, Paper Tiger joins a lot of movies this year that can be labelled as good, but maybe not great. It’s worth a watch if you’re into crime dramas and want one with some top-notch acting, but I don’t think you’ll be wowed by much else due to the familiarity of the narrative beats and tropes.

title: Is ‘Wildwood’ Safe For Kids? A Parent’s Spoiler-Free Review – ScreenHub Entertainment
content:
The film Wildwood has been causing a bit of a stir online, and not just because of the stunning visuals and groundbreaking multimedia artistry. Rather, it’s because a segment of parents decided to disregard the PG13 rating and take their children to see this stop-motion spectacle, not expecting some of the darker themes in the film. I was one of those parents, and I’d like to explain exactly why I am extremely happy that I took my son to see Wildwood.

Editor’s Note: The author has attempted to avoid spoilers, but does include some vague descriptions of events in the film.

The Plot

A young woman named Prue discovers a world of magic and fantasy hidden just outside the city limits of Portland, Oregon. Prue and her reluctant friend Curtis will face extreme danger, thrilling adventure, and the scourge of municipal bureaucracy in their quest to save her baby brother from a powerful sorceress driven mad by grief.

The Rating

Wildwood earned a PG-13 rating from the MPAA, and I understand why. One of the opening scenes in the film deals with suicide in a very fantastical way and, while not exactly graphic, it is definitely not subtle. Later in the story, there are some large-scale battles that display equally large-scale violence.

Though the PG-13 rating is warranted, that shouldn’t be the only thing to consider when deciding whether or not to take your child to see it. It’s true that the MPAA rating can be a valuable tool. However, sometimes it is exactly because of those “adult” themes that you should watch these movies with your children.

Can Kids Handle It?

One of the most important lessons that a parent can learn is that every child is different. So, when considering if your child can handle any film, regardless of rating or subject, it is your responsibility to judge whether your child has the ability to understand what they will see on screen.

For any parents who are unsure about Wildwood, I wrote a detailed description of ways to assess your child’s tolerance and prepare them for possible mature subjects when the film Beatlejuice Beatlejuice came out. Among other things, I evaluated my son’s ability to separate fiction from reality, explained what he could expect, and made sure he had snacks to mentally ground him.

Start the Conversation

The fact that the film Wildwood contains some delicate subjects, but is still packaged in such an accessible medium, gives parents a unique opportunity. In a 2016 interview with USA Today, Wildwood director Travis Knight said: “We respect that children are smart, sophisticated and can handle things that adults typically don’t think they can.” Despite what many think, this holds true even for subjects such as depression, grief, and suicide.

These subjects are not exclusive to adults, and stories like Wildwood give parents the opportunity to introduce these harsh concepts in a safe setting. More often than not, it is the parents who aren’t ready to talk about these subjects with their children, but it can be extremely important to try before they are confronted with them in the real world.

The temptation to protect our children from anything that might disturb them is a strong one. We always want to do what’s best for them, but sometimes what’s best for them is uncomfortable for us. We must be able to speak with our kids about difficult realities to prepare them for life. In this regard, I believe Laika Studios has done parents a great service in Wildwood.

title: ‘Wildwood’ is a Must-See – ScreenHub Entertainment
content:
More than a dozen times over the course of watching Wildwood, the latest film from Laika Studios, I caught myself thinking, “How the hell did they even make this movie?” It’s been a long time since I’ve been utterly transported by a movie, both in terms of imagination, spectacle, and craft, and yet Wildwood did just that. I didn’t bury the lede here: Wildwood is a must-see cinematic event.

Directed by Travis Knight and written by Chris Butler (both responsible for Kubo and the Two Strings), Wildwood follows a teenage girl from Portland named Prue, who, against the wishes of her parents, brings her infant brother outdoors for some fun in town despite the express instructions not to do so. Of course, she should have listened to her parents, as magical forces from beyond the Impassable Wilderness abduct her brother and bring him into the forest, a place where no one from the outside world can get in due to an impassable network of vines and trees. Yet Prue is somehow able to breach the barrier, and with the help of Curtis, a shy, dorky classmate of hers, they venture into the magical realm beyond the trees.

Much like Kubo and Coraline, Wildwood is a stop-motion animated film. Unlike those films, I forgot constantly throughout the film that it was a stop-motion animated film. The animation and attention to detail are so smooth and lifelike, removing that traditional jankiness that’s associated with the medium. Characters are lifelike and expressive, reacting to events with subtle ticks and reactions, even tearing up (this is stop-motion, don’t forget, no CG like Pixar), so little details like that really stand out. I would recommend watching this behind the scenes to fully understand the magic.

From an art/production standpoint, I must say I really love the look and feel of this movie. There are stylistic elements from the medieval period, the 18th or 19th century, and early 20th century here, creating this unique hodgepodge of costumes and architectural designs. The world is inhabited by both humans and anthropomorphic animals, most notably the coyotes, who serve the Dowager Countess Alexandra, the film’s primary antagonist. Voiced by Carey Mulligan, the Countess could’ve easily been a one-dimensional villain hellbent on just doing villainous things, but Wildwood fleshes out her backstory with tragic detail. Wildwood succeeds not only with its art and visuals, but by having a complex and layered story on top of it.

As a note: this may be an animated movie, but I would advise against bringing young children. Wildwood is a dark film, with some thematic elements that may scare younger kids. The movie opens, and you’re instantly left traumatized. There’s some frightening images too, and it doesn’t shy away from violence. There’s some humour to help lift the mood, but it never compromises the drama in any way, thankfully. But I would not call this a “light” movie at all. But kids (and parents) who are open to exploring these themes and elements have a great outlet here. As always, it’s up to the parents to gauge what is safe. Just don’t go into this one expecting a family-friendly experience the whole way. This is very much a PG-13 movie in the end.

If I did have a criticism of the film, it would be that it does resolve things fairly quickly by the end. I would’ve liked to have a bit more rumination on what happened and why. The film elects to just wrap itself up, but considering everything we just went through, I think a bit of time for Prue and Curtis to reflect with the allies they made along the way and the weight of what just happened.

As Prue and Curtis explore and learn about the world they’re now inhabiting, they discover kingdoms, magical beings, talking animals, and see vast armies clash. The scope of this movie, more than once, reminded me of The Lord of the Rings, by way of Redwall and a dash of Princess Mononoke. It’s incredibly imaginative, and knowing that so much of this movie was made by hand is fascinating and only increases that sense of awe.

Wildwood is one of those films that utterly transports you. It’s a film that was clearly made by a team of passionate artists who poured years of their lives into making this film. I would strongly encourage you to not only watch it, but to go out and support it. In an age where so many films feel soulless and bland, Wildwood is anything but.

title: ‘Street Fighter’ Review – ScreenHub Entertainment
content:
If you’re a fan of 90s fighting games, you’re a winner this year. Not only did we have Mortal Kombat II this year,  but the latest attempt to give us an authentic Street Fighter movie just hit the big screen. Does this one work or should it have stayed off the big screen? Let’s find out.

As a note,  unlike Mortal Kombat, I have no real experience or nostalgia for Street Fighter. I may have played quite a bit of the former, but haven’t played much of the latter. I know some of the overall basics, and the design of many others due to their cultural impact,  but for all intents and purposes, I’m going into this not as a fan.

Street Fighter largely follows the story of Ryu and Ken, two best friends who were trained together in Japan by Master Gouken. Ryu is a natural talent and is the inaugural winner of the World Warrior Tournament, with Ken sitting it out for being Ryu’s training partner. But not long after his victory, he vanished, and Ken has become a wannabe has-been who does easy fights only for fame and money. But when M. Bison launches the Second Tournament, fighters from across the world are brought in to compete, and the question everyone is asking is: will Ryu and Ken finally get to face off?

Street Fighter is definitely a mixed one. It does some things really well, and some things end up feeling quite messy.

So let’s start with the positive. The cast is overall quite good for this material,  with everyone seemingly understanding the assignment of camp and zaniness. Ryu and Ken are definitely the leads, so they get the most to do, and often the movie finds a good rhythm in exploring their relationship and fallout. I really think the movie should’ve focused more on this aspect of the movie, as this is the heart and the more engaging aspect. The other fighters are largely just there in the background as one-dimensional inclusions, but they’re still on point, especially Cody Rhodes as Guile; he just leans into the silliness of it all. The costumes also feel lovingly recreated from the games. The movie also features 2D animated flashback sequences, and these parts straight up rule, to the point where I think the whole movie should’ve been like this.  They’re far more convincing and engrossing than the live-action sequences.

Street Fighter is set in the 90s and also boasts a really fun 90s soundtrack. It may not make a lick of sense in terms of the years of release, as the film takes place in 1993, but that’s a bridge I can get over if it means we get the likes of 2Pac, Offspring, 4 Non Blondes, Too $hort, and Soundgarden in the movie.

While the cast may have realized their parts well, it’s ironic that the best actor in the movie is also the one who struggles the most. David Dastmalchian plays Bison and is definitely miscast in the role. He lacks the menace to come off as a scary villain, but can’t chew the scenery enough to make it a fun villain either. It’s never fair to compare, but from what I’ve seen of the 1994 version, Raul Julia gives a far more convincing turn as Bison, as he treated the role as he would any other role, with complete class. Dastmalchian’s turn feels very one-dimensional, flat, and boring by contrast. It’s a shame, as Dastmalchian is such a good talent in general.

The movie is also a bit of a mess in the edit. There were a few instances where the movie jarringly jumps ahead without offering any context or explanation; there’s just missing scenes in the movie, and we’re expected to deduce why this one character who was captured one scene ago is now free, for instance. The movie also relies a bit too much on humour, much like the Masters of the Universe film, and sometimes it can derail the movie. There’s an awful lot of Eric André in this movie, at the expense of a lot of the other fighters, for instance.

There’s also not a lot of the tournament, with most of those fights happening off-screen, and that feels like the same mistake the 2021 Mortal Kombat made. I would’ve focused on the tournament and Ryu and Ken’s relationship, rather than Bison’s whole quest to look for Psycho Power. There’s a lot going on in this movie, between Chung Li’s (Callina Liang) recruitment and secret mission, Ryu’s darkness, Ken’s comeback, Bison’s master plan, and the more supernatural element of the demon Akuma (Roman Reigns). Street Fighter also abruptly ends, not even with a cliffhanger perse, but it builds up momentum and simply pulls the cord at a baffling spot. I guess the studio is hoping for a sequel.

So I’d say if you’re a fan of the games, or are jonesing for a 90s throwback movie both in style and execution, you may have some fun after checking your brain at the door. It’s got style, and some fun camp to be had, but I also feel it was messy and was trying to do too many things at once.

title: ‘Trust Me, I’m a Doctor’: Director Thane Economou on Working with Kal Penn, Abbie Cornish, and Bringing This True Story to Life
content:
Kal Penn’s latest film, Trust Me, I’m a Doctor, is a wild ride from start to finish. Part biopic, part true crime, and mostly laugh-out-loud comedy follows the real-life journey of Dr. Sandeep Kapoor, a simple doctor with a small practice in the San Fernando Valley, whose life is turned upside down when he is implicated in the death of reality star Anna Nicole Smith. I sat down with Thane Economou, the writer/director of Trust Me, I’m a Doctor, to talk about his motivations and experiences making the film.

How did this start? How did Trust Me, I’m a Doctor come to be?

Thane Economou: My producer, Ryan Hawkins, had the rights to the book, the memoir that it’s based on, and he handed it over to me. We worked together in the past, and he said, “Can you make heads or tails of this? Do you have a take on this?” I got the book, and to be completely honest, I looked at the cover: Trust Me, I’m a Doctor: My Life Before and After Anna Nicole Smith. I said, “I don’t know if this is going to be for me. I don’t know what this is. It’s going to be salacious.”

Then I start reading it, and about 30 pages in, Anna Nicole Smith passes away. It’s utterly heartbreaking, but I’m looking at the rest of the book and wondering, what else is here? What’s this gonna be? And what it ended up being was a truth-is-crazier-than-fiction trial that Dr. Kapoor gets sucked into. I end up discovering this character of Dr. Kapoor, this extremely flawed, extremely human character who keeps on making mistakes and tripping over his own feet into holes he keeps digging for himself, and I found it to be a fascinating character, an interesting story, and a really interesting world to explore, which was like this 2007 height of tabloid culture media circus trial that includes everything from the highest offices in the California government, all the way down to Harvey Lemon of TMZ. I just wanted to jump in, so I raised my hand and said, “I want this”, and started writing almost immediately.

At what point did you decide that it was gonna be a comedy? Because this could have been a very serious true crime film.

Thane Economou: For me, it was about replicating the experience I had reading the memoir. Some things that occurred in real life were so wild that I was chuckling to myself. I find Kapoor, through his own self-deprecating self-awareness, to be quite a funny character. And yet there are these elements within the story that are heartbreaking and full of despair. I felt that showing the full breadth of those emotions in the story was important. That was something, from moment one, I said, “If I’m going to tell this, I’m going to tell this the way that I would tell this story at a cocktail party.” 

I want to make sure that people understand the stakes of it and how truly dark some of the moments got. But at the other end of the spectrum, this is a funny story. Even if we’re just talking about Anna Nicole Smith, she was fun, she was funny, she was full of light, she was full of brightness. I wanted, especially in those early parts of the film, to display what it would have felt like to be in her orbit, which would have been quite the fun thing. So, to me, it was about capturing all the emotions I felt when I was reading it for the first time.

I was thinking about the way the film humanizes Anna Nicole Smith. She had this persona of the party girl, the blonde bombshell, the dumb blonde that she really leaned into. But the way she wound up being treated was very unfair. I think it was well handled in the film.

Thane Economou: Well, thank you. It’s a responsibility whenever you write anything that’s based on a true person. And with Anna Nicole Smith, specifically with Anna, I read every single memoir or biography that I could about her or that she was included in. I watched her entire filmography. I watched all of The Anna Nicole Show. I watched basically any interview I could, and what I discovered was someone who was extremely complex. As I say in the film, she is a hard person to pin down and to know fully, and part of that is because she’s just so human. She was a three-dimensional person, and I wanted to display her that way. 

One of the things I say about Anna Nicole is that she had the same ups and downs as all of us; she just lived a life of more extremes. This was someone who was just full of life. In her happy moments, she was so full of love and so loving to all the people around her; that’s what you would always hear from people who met her. And yet her moments of heartbreak are more devastating than any that I’ve ever encountered, in my research or in my life.

The other side of that equation was the moment that Abbie Cornish came on board to play her. Abbie said from moment one that she felt that she knew this character from the inside. She knew people who had lived lives like Anna, who had suffered like Anna, people who had died of prescription drug overdoses. She knew that she wanted to honor that, and in a lot of ways, Abbie became my Anna defender, my Anna whisperer, the person who was at every turn pulling us back to the truth and saying, “Okay, but what would Anna have really done here? What did Anna really do here? What did she really say here?” 

I opened the film with an interview with Abbie as Anna Nicole Smith. In the original script, I’d written a fictional interview. A fictional thing that I felt encapsulated her. Abbie was the one who said, “No. We have one of the most photographed, one of the most videoed people of all time.” So she went through, and she found one from 1994. She said, “What I’d like to do is record this interview word for word. Then you, Thane, can use this as B-roll and cut it up however you want. And that’s what we ended up doing. So at every turn, Abbie just said, “Let’s go to the truth. Let’s go to what was real.” And I really think that helped draw that three-dimensional picture of Anna.

I wanted to ask you about Abbie Cornish, because Kal Penn is awesome, but Abbie Cornish melts into this character. What’s it like working with somebody like that?

Thane Economou: It was very cool, and at times a little eerie. How Abbie came to be Anna was through research and voice training, but she would also spend about 3-plus hours in hair and makeup and costume before she would ever arrive on set. Oftentimes, we’d have to prep our Anna scenes, totally, have it all lit with stand-ins, everything. We were ready to rock and roll. Then we’d go shoot something with Kal. 

The moment that we heard “Abbie’s on her way, Abbie’s out of hair and makeup”, we would run over and get ready, because she would have to perform her scenes and then immediately go back in hair and makeup for another setup, and then another setup. So our time with Abbie on set ended up being limited, but highly powerful. When she walked on set, she was in character, and she was in hair and makeup, and in order to kind of keep that voice, she was in the voice at all times. It felt a lot of times like we were being joined by Anna, and it’s kind of nerdy, but I caught myself on occasion calling her Anna. It felt right. That process, I think, really elevated her performance. She was able to, for however long she was on set, remain completely in character.

A film can really live or die on its secondary characters, and I thought Trust Me, I’m a Doctor was very well cast. The dad and the woman who Dr. Kapoor was treating throughout the whole film. She provided a wonderful through-line and was beautifully written. What was it like looking for the right people for those roles?

Thane Economou: It was a long process. You’re right, they’re smaller roles, but with a cast like this, an ensemble, it’s so important, especially with those more emotional roles. Characters that have those emotional throughlines. You have to get it right. 

Dhrindra plays Sandeep’s father. That is an actor with an incredible resume of stage, film, and television that I had never seen really be able to do this much on screen before. So, working with him, I was blown away by his level of research. He held several conversations with the real Mr. Kapoor, and felt that that level of authenticity was important. He would have conversations with Kal about their dynamics as father and son, and I just remember, especially in that final scene between the two of them, remarking that it was beautiful work. I was just honored to have been in the room for that.

The actress who plays Margie, his elderly patient, is another character actor we discovered who was so completely there. It’s to her credit, Jocelyn Zuko, who plays her, that it becomes such an emotional through-line, and very important to giving the film that heart. She really helps connect you with Dr. Kapoor to see what he’s like with one of his patients. That was really great. 

From there, it was a murderer’s row of smaller roles that were filled with actors that truly came in ready to knock it out of the park. Another one being Elon Gold, who plays Harvey Levin, just completely immersed himself and said, “I’m gonna give you the ultimate Harvey Levin”, to the point where, after the screening, someone walked up to me and asked, “Was that the real Harvey Levin?” I said, ” No, that’s an actor.

David Julian Hirsch’s Howard K. Stern was another one. I couldn’t believe what he was delivering in his scenes. That came from him finding the footage, immersing himself in it, and just really feeling Howard K. Stern from the inside out.

That scene between Dr. Kapoor and his father was really emotional and really beautiful. To be able to put that together and give them what they need to bring that to life, how much of that is from the director?

Thane Economou: Oh, I’ll push it off myself and say that that scene, that emotional final scene between father and son, was truly collaborative. It was the hardest scene I had to write. It’s a credit to Kal working with me on the scene and constantly helping me tweak it, and of course the performances that elevated it. But also, Kal went back to Dr. Kapoor and had conversations with him about how this scene played out in real life, in ways that were included in the final script. So it really starts with the page, but at a certain point, everyone gets their fingers in it, and it just becomes better and stronger.

Is there something that feels relevant about this film? In today’s world, we have influencers, and social media can propel somebody to insane levels of fame almost instantly. Do you think Trust Me, I’m a Doctor has any messages or lessons?

Thane Economou: I feel like I wanted to speak to this moment in time, 2005 to 2007. That felt like the proto-everything we’re living in now in terms of social media and celebrity culture. It felt like at the time that there was one Anna Nicole Smith and one Harvey Levin, and now it feels like there’s 10 million wannabe Anna Nicole Smiths and 10 million wannabe Harvey Levins. 

We could see the way that this celebrity culture was permeating into everything, including government and the justice system. One of the things that I talk about in this case is how the person that was leading the charge on Dr. Kapoor’s court case was Attorney General Jerry Brown, who was running for governor, and boy, wouldn’t this be a good piece of television to have Anna Nicole Smith’s doctors on trial.

The ways in which Harvey Levin is gaining power and gaining access and all of those things felt like they were bubbling up to the surface. The Anna Nicole Show was effectively, for all intents and purposes, the first major celebrity reality show. Now we’ve not only moved beyond everyone having a reality show to everyone’s Instagram account effectively being their reality show. So, I really just wanted to take that moment in time and look at how our current culture was kind of being seeded in some ways.

Before we sign off, I just have a quick question. Other than Trust Me, I’m a Doctor, what is your favorite Kal Penn movie?

Thane Economou: The Namesake. That was the one where I came in and knew Kal was right for the role. Because I knew he could obviously do comedy, and I knew he was this comforting screen presence that was important for people to identify with. But as far as the dramatic work went, I knew from the namesake that he is a tremendously talented actor with incredible depth. Knowing what he was capable of in The Namesake, I said, “I need him for this role”.

Trust Me, I’m a Doctor is based on Dr. Kapoor’s own memoir and will be in theaters October 16th.

title: Is ‘The Social Reckoning’ Worth Seeing? – ScreenHub Entertainment
content:
The Social Network is considered by many to be an exemplary piece of cinema. We ranked it quite high on our coverage of the best films of the century thus far, so the pressure was certainly on for its quasi-sequel, The Social Reckoning. Can it live up to the legacy of the first film, and , better question, can it stand on its own? Let’s find out.

The Social Reckoning stars Mikey Madison as Frances Haugen, a data engineer over at Facebook who becomes disenfranchised with her employer over how the company has changed how people use the platform. She’s discovered that Facebook’s new algorithm seems to be feeding on hate and negative content and perhaps even radicalizing users. Unfortunately, no one internally wants to stir the pot on this topic, which leads her to cross paths with The Wall Street Journal’s new tech writer, Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White). Despite his job title, he knows very little about tech, but has made a name for himself in D.C. as a political investigative journalist, something he hopes to channel into his investigation of Facebook.

The Social Network director David Fincher sits this spiritual sequel out, allowing that film’s writer, Aaron Sorkin, to pull double duty as both director and writer. Sorkin, love him or hate him, is a pretty reputable writer, but his directing efforts haven’t quite hit the same pedigree as his other projects. Reckoning continues that trend. It’s not like he’s a bad director, but compared to someone like Fincher, he just lacks a lot of style and flair, opting for a safer and risk-free directorial approach. Scriptwise, this entry actually feels a bit more restrained for a Sorkin picture. Yes, there is impossible dialogue, as is traditional, but it feels a bit more checked in. I had recently watched The Social Network in anticipation of this film, and that movie’s dialogue feels more quippy and rapid-fire than this one’s.

Unlike Network, Reckoning isn’t a start-up story about ambitious geniuses, but a journalism story chronicling The Wall Street Journal’s 17-part series, The Facebook Files. It also taps into the platform’s policies and impact during the January 6 Insurrection and the COVID pandemic, but they do feel more like footnotes. I think a six-part mini-series for the three years covered over the course of the movie may have allowed some of these beats to be explored more in depth. There’s a lot going on in this movie, from exploring the dark secrets of Facebook to the whistleblower and investigative angle.

Everyone in the movie does solid work. Allen White is good as Horowitz, perhaps not straying too far from his turn as Carmine in The Bear. Mikey Madison fares better as Frances, an unpopular employee at Facebook who sees value in a platform like Facebook, but questions the direction the company is going. Bill Burr shows up as a fictitious character who sort of serves as the moral compass, challenging the status quo, and Burr actually may be the highlight of the whole film, verbally sparring with Strong’s Zuckberg constantly. Also in the movie, but not as much as you might think, is Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg, taking over from Jesse Eisenberg. Strong plays the role wonderfully, tapping into that robotic cadence and mannerisms that sometimes make Zuckerberg feel unapproachable at best, or unlikeable at worst. Zuck isn’t really a character here, unlike the first movie, but rather the poster child for the problems at the company. Strong plays the role well, but don’t expect to learn much about the Facebook CEO in this movie. This isn’t about him.

Atticus Ross and Trent Reznor do not return to score this one, so Alexandre Desplat gives us a fresh new sound for this entry, and I, for one, missed the unsettling and understated score from Social Network. Desplat’s work is good, but it feels at odds with the more nihilistic and grim reality Reckoning presents. The score can sometimes veer into hopeful optimism, as if there’s a light at the end of the tunnel, and it feels tonally out of place. Reckoning also shares the same cinematographer as The Social Network, Jeff Cronenweth, but surprisingly, the two movies don’t look or feel anything alike; I was surprised to learn it was the same person responsible for the photography.

The realist in me wonders if “Reckoning” was really the best title for this movie. There isn’t really one in the real world, or in the movie, as Facebook (now Meta) is still around and valued more than it was just a few years ago. The Empire wins, but the movie presents itself as more optimistic, as if its mission will in turn inspire users to question the apps they so passionately cling to. Judging by the box office for the film, this is unlikely to be the case.

The question then becomes: did this movie ultimately justify its existence? In a way. I do think the message of informing people about the findings of the WSJ is commendable, as many people likely skipped it, but the movie may also be too late for anyone to care. Meta may be raking in the dough, but Facebook itself is not the powerhouse it used to be socially anymore. Perhaps this could’ve looked at a different platform, taken a more anthological approach. Also, AI is the new thing, for better or worse, and social media companies are further intergrating into this tech. The question now isn’t whether Facebook is addictive or manipulative, but is AI going to take my job or go rogue.

So to answer my initial question: is The Social Reckoning worth seeing? Overall, I think so. It’s a good movie, with solid performances from its cast, a sharp script, and it feels informative. But it’s also maybe a few years too late and lacks the cinematic flair that its predecessor had, which keeps it from being a great movie. So if you’re into investigations, or don’t know about the Facebook Files, I would say this is a good companion to Network, but it isn’t the cultural touchstone that movie was. Is it unfair to compare the two? Maybe a little, but they are spiritual sequels and share the same writer, so comparison is inevitable.

title: ‘Obsession’ Spoiler-Free Review – ScreenHub Entertainment
content:
Finally! At long last, we have a review for Obsession on the site. It feels like it’s been a long time coming. We’ve seen so many movies this year, but one of the most buzzed-about ones simply passed us by. But with the spooky season upon us, and it being available on streaming, it seemed like a good time to check it out finally. Was it worth the hype when it came out, or was it all overblown? Let’s find out.

Obsession, made for a paltry $750,000, features a small cast of unknowns and only a few locations, and yet it feels bigger and bolder than many of its big-budget contemporaries. It stars Michael Johnston as Bear, a shy, awkward 20-something-year-old who works at a local music store. He has all the feels for Nikki (Inde Navarrette), his coworker who sees him more as a friend than as someone worth dating, despite them getting along really well. After shopping for a gift for her comes up short, he buys a One Wish Willow on a whim and wishes that she’ll love him more than anyone in the world. Moments later, Nikki returns to him, seemingly a whole new person, open to the idea of a romantic future with Bear. But as the old adage says, be careful what you wish for.

Despite not being billed by A-listers, Obsession shines with its cast. The acting in the film is quite good, from Bear flip-flopping between acceptance, fear, and denial over and over again, and Navarrette’s completely batshit crazy turn as Nikki, someone who seemingly loves someone so blindly and passionately that she’ll go to any extreme to hold and preserve that love, even when it’s not real. Take away the supernatural angle, and it’s a very interesting look at toxic relationships on its own.

But this is also a horror movie. Even with its smaller budget, Obsession delivers thanks to the great role Navarette gives for Nikki, a completely unhinged and terrifying performance. But the film also boasts some very effective lighting, often drenching Nikki in complete darkness, reducing her to nothing more than a silhouette or a mass. It also takes some big, disturbing swings that’ll likely make you feel very

In the end, I found Obsession was very much worth the hype. It was well-acted, well-shot, insightful, disturbing, and exceeded my expectations. Worth a watch this Halloween season if you’ve yet to check it out!

title: Lanterns: ‘Dirt and Stars’ & Overall Season Review – ScreenHub Entertainment
content:
Apologies once again for the weird release of articles of Lanterns. I did miss out on last week’s review, and now the finale is coming to you later than anticipated. Let’s rectify that in this article, and also give you my thoughts on the season now that the show has come to an end. Did it live up to the promise of being True Detective meets DC, or did the show misfire? Let’s find out.

A quick summary of the previous episode first, that said. I thought having a different version of Hal accompany John throughout the episode was a clever way of keeping Kyle Chandler in the show, despite the ticking clock of the ring’s limited “battery” time left. The episode was also the most “cosmic” of the show to date, with a wormhole to a far-off planet ravaged by fear. It’s also where Sinestro has been hiding, after he was sprung out of jail. I feel we could’ve used more Sinestro overall, and more cosmic detours to help make Lanterns feel more unique. John also got over the whole fear thing really quick, despite it clearly affecting his mind as they were on the boat heading towards the lighthouse.

Onto the finale. Now, did I call Noah being the Manhunter, or did I not call that? Perhaps it was pretty easily telegraphed; genetic lineage isn’t a huge assumption, but it was nice to see it unfold. What was even better was how Noah was challenging his very nature. He’s aware of the corrupting nature of his alien heritage and fears that he’ll end up doing something bad as a result. Knowing that John mercy-killed his grandmother ten years ago, he asked John for the same; just after his final football game. Noah even confesses to the murder of Hal to try and tempt John, but our Lantern protege knows better: it was Kerry Kane all along who killed Hal. Not in cold blood, but in a desperate move upon learning that Hal knew her son was the same alien threat that came to town all those years ago. To protect her son, she killed Hal, and it’s something John deduced for himself after learning that Noah was a Manhunter and one who may be better than his programming. The best scene in the episode, arguably in the show, was when John and Noah shared a car ride to the football game, where the topic of nature versus nurture, mercy, and consequence really became paramount. Thankfully for him, John has a moral compass and refuses to execute a teenager, especially when there’s a chance for a better tomorrow. So not turning this into a CGI battle like so many other superhero tales was a welcome change.

By the end, John assumes the mantle of Green Lantern and coerces Guy Gardner to give up Earth in exchange for the stars. John will operate as a sort of independent contractor, not bound by the whim of the Guardians and their messy history, but solely as someone who is in it to protect Earth. I wonder if we’ll see Pierre show up on the big screen or in a second season? (Lanterns hasn’t been renewed yet for a second season). A DCU without Hal Jordan also feels, weird, if I’m being honest. So we’ll see how this future turns out.

So did the show work overall? Yes, but it also felt like it was still missing something. Aaron Pierre crushed it as John, which is interesting since he was so stoic throughout. He paired nicely with Chandler’s rough-around-the-edges Hal Jordan, but I feel the show could’ve done more in the way of actual detective work. It felt like half the time they simply stumbled into a scenario by fluke or by ease. I never felt like there was a major challenge or roadblock for them to face, apart from each other. John gets a bit more thanks to the ample backstory with his family, but that’s to serve his character arc, and not the overall mystery. It so clearly wants to be True Detective, but it also feels like a sanitized version of that iconic show instead of trying to do something more novel and original. Taking that concept and setting it in a more sci-fi setting could’ve really made this more unique, but the small-town setting, the hunt, it did feel familiar to a fault. It didn’t help that the show felt very predictable at times too. I mentioned that I called Noah, and Zoe was hardly a big surprise twist. So while Lanterns was great in the drama and character department, its overall mystery felt lacking. Would I watch another season, though? Probably, if only because Pierre did great work in the lead role. So overall, Lanterns was a solid character story about a man brought up in extreme circumstances and alienated by his family, but also a so-so mystery story. It’s a decent show overall, just not an amazing one. And considering the bar set by HBO, I think the show could’ve been better.

title: ‘Heart of the Beast’ Spoiler-Free Review – ScreenHub Entertainment
content:
Director David Ayer and Brad Pitt team up once again, but instead of showcasing the horrors of war like they did in Fury, they’re offering a much smaller-scale movie in The Heart of the Beast. Pitt may be the lead actor, but it’s his canine co-star who steals the movie in this surprisingly good survival movie. 

As mentioned, Pitt stars as James Belmont, a retired Green Beret who ventures into the Alaskan wilderness with Odin, a retired combat German Shepherd who is also James’ best friend. We don’t get too much backstory on James, enough to know that both he and Odin have been through hell while they served,  and seem much more content with a solitary life with each other’s company. After their plane crashes in the middle of the wilderness, James and Odin have to trek some 58 miles to the nearest road, braving the elements and wilderness.

Apart from J.K. Simmons appearing early on as a retired prospector, pretty much all of the movie stays with James and Odin. The movie ends up being light on dialogue, but that doesn’t mean the movie is lacking. It ends up saying quite a lot about the unconditional love between man and dog, in a way that doesn’t feel manipulative to the audience. Pitt also gives a really strong performance as James, tapping into that love despite being a man clearly haunted by his past.

But it’s Uber, the main dog playing Odin, who steals the movie. I don’t know how they got such a performance from this animal, but they really succeeded in making Odin a character. Most notable are his eyes, which are extremely expressive, to the point where we know what Odin is thinking in any given scene, and we quickly become very protective of this canine as a result. Like James, Odin has seen hell while working as a combat dog, and suffers from PTSD induced nightmares, which only strengthens the bond between him and James. No one else knows their struggle, but they have each other. Helping Uber bring Odin to life are three other dogs, filling in for stunts and other stand-in shots, and thankfully, the other three canines are Uber’s own sons. When Odin is sad, we fully know it based on how Uber is acting and how the cinematography captures the dog.

The movie is also gorgeously shot, with New Zealand doubling as Alaska. Yes, I thought about Middle-earth more than a few times, but the soaring vistas and natural beauty are hard to ignore and easy to appreciate. There’s some iffy VFX here and there with other animals, but it never took me out of the movie too much. What did take me out more was the infrequent flashbacks to James’ time in the war. They didn’t add anything we couldn’t deduce ourselves and broke up the flow of the survival narrative.

Heart of the Beast doesn’t reinvent the wheel; it taps into tropes and themes we’ve seen done in other dog and/or survival movies before. But it does it with such earnest heart and warmth that it’s hard not to get wrapped up in the wonder of it all. I think this one will make the waterworks flow for dog lovers, but it can make non-dog lovers feel warm and fuzzy thanks to the compassionate relationship shown between Odin and James. For a tight 90-min survival romp featuring nice vistas, the best boy, and a great turn by Pitt, you could do worse with this one.
